title: Tales from the Loop - Board Gaming in an '80s that Never Was
body:
https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=r4YE2Zghgbc

Daniel (@dungeondive) takes a look at the Tales from the Loop board game, which grew out of an art book, then a lore book, then Free League's RPG on the Mutant Year Zero engine, a system he has played extensively and likes. The pitch is Scooby-Doo meets The X-Files meets Stranger Things in an alternate 1980s where particle accelerators in Sweden and the United States let strange things through. Two to five players run high-school archetypes; he is playing Nils the weirdo and Clara the bookworm, whose iconic starting items are a lowrider bike and a pack of chewing gum. Items combine, so gum plus a hockey stick yields a club with reach.

What he admires is how relentlessly the game models being a kid. Rounds are school days, each opening with a school event such as a substitute teacher you can charm into letting you leave early. Weekly chore cards reward or punish you. Asking your parents for a ride costs favour, missing dinner costs more, and getting grounded locks two of your action cubes. Sentry robots patrol the map, switching between routine and alert, and can be hacked and ridden. He is playing the Mystery Islands sandbox, filming for the video club on a new VHS camera.

The rulebook, though, is surprisingly poor for Free League, with real ambiguity around the robots. His verdict: not one of the better adventure games, but one of the most thematic, worth bumbling through if the 1980s appeal.

----

This game makes parental favour, chores and getting grounded into core mechanisms. Which board game has best captured the texture of ordinary life alongside its adventure?
